deep.reconstruction:
Context (Ch. 12, Tractatus de numerorum doctrina): p = 4q+1 is prime and R = {1, α, β, γ, ...} is the set of biquadratic (fourth-power) residues mod p. By §421, R = {a : a^q ≡ 1}, and R is closed under multiplication. By §426, x is chosen so that x^2 is a quadratic residue but not in R. Then x and x^3 are not in R. Three classes of non-residues are formed: I = xR, II = x^2R, III = x^3R. All computations below are mod p.

§427: Each class has |R| = n elements. Within a class the elements are distinct, since x is invertible mod a prime (implicit).

§428 (the classes are disjoint):
- If αx ≡ βx^2, then x(βx − α) ≡ 0, so βx ≡ α ∈ R. Hence βx ∈ R, but βx lies in class I, a contradiction.
- If αx ≡ βx^3, then α ≡ βx^2 ∈ R, a contradiction.
- If αx^2 ≡ βx^3, then α ≡ βx ∈ R, a contradiction.
(Implicit, mine: cancelling x uses that p is prime and p ∤ x. The disjointness of I, II, III from R itself was settled in §426.)

§429: So there are at least 3n non-residues. If these three classes exhaust them, then n + 3n = 4n = p − 1 = 4q, so n = q.

§430 (multiplication table of the cosets, using x^4 ∈ R and closure of R):
- I·I ⊂ II and III·III ⊂ II (x^6 = x^4·x^2).
- II·II ⊂ R and I·III ⊂ R.
- I·II ⊂ III.
- II·III ⊂ I (x^5 = x^4·x).
In modern terms this is the cyclic group Z/4 acting on the cosets of R in (Z/p)^*.

§431: A square s = t^2 cannot lie in I or III, because s·s = t^4 ∈ R, whereas I·I and III·III lie in II. Euler concludes that squares lie only in R ∪ II, so the number of squares is 2n.

§432: If R ∪ II contains all quadratic residues, of which there are 2q (shown earlier), then 2n = 2q. Hence 4n = 4q, the four classes fill all of 1..4q, and n = q.

§433: The doubt is therefore reduced to excluding a square non-residue y^2 outside II. If one existed, it would generate three new classes, giving 6n non-residues, and, if complete, 7n = 4q.

§434: The new classes are IV = yR, V = y^2R, VI = y^3R, each with n terms. Two cases are to be examined: xy ∈ R or xy ∉ R.

§435 (case xy ∈ R):
- Then x·IV = xyR ⊂ R gives n residues.
- Also x·III = x^4R ⊂ R gives n residues.
- These two sets are disjoint: αxy ≡ βx^4 implies αy ≡ βx^3, putting αy in class III, contrary to the hypothesis that IV is a new class.
- So R would contain 2n distinct elements, which is absurd. Hence xy ∉ R.
The other case, and the conclusion n = q, are handled on the next page.
errors: §431 asserts flatly that only class II (with R) contains squares and that the number of squares is 2n. As stated, this presupposes that all non-residues lie in I–III; squares could a priori lie in further classes. Euler himself recognises the gap in §§432–433 and repairs it in §§434ff., so it is a presentational overstatement, not a final error.
§428 is elliptical: 'foret βx^2 − αx' lacks 'divisibile per 4q+1' (as in the printed text). The cancellation of x tacitly uses that p is prime and p does not divide x.
§435: x·III = x^4R is in fact R itself, since x^4 ∈ R. The argument is correct but roundabout; it amounts to: xy ∈ R ⇒ y ∈ x^{-1}R = x^3R = III, a contradiction.

results.what: For prime p = 4q+1, the fourth-power residues R form a multiplicative set whose cosets xR, x^2R, x^3R (with x^2 ∉ R) are pairwise disjoint, each of size |R|. This gives a coset multiplication table isomorphic to Z/4.
results.modern_name: Cosets of the subgroup of 4th powers in (Z/p)^*; quotient (Z/p)^*/((Z/p)^*)^4 ≅ Z/4; Lagrange-type coset counting
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (coset argument for power residues, E262/E449, c. 1758–1772); group-theoretic formulation later (Gauss, Disquisitiones 1801; Galois/Jordan)

results.what: Number of biquadratic residues mod 4q+1 is exactly q, proved by showing all non-residues fall into three classes (excluding further square non-residues outside x^2R).
results.modern_name: Index of 4th powers in (Z/p)^* equals gcd(4, p−1) = 4
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (Tractatus de numerorum doctrina, c. 1750s; published posthumously 1849); Gauss for the general theory

results.what: Squares lie only in R ∪ x^2R; squares of class-I/III elements land in class II.
results.modern_name: Quadratic residues = subgroup of index 2 containing the index-4 subgroup

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's known coset-style treatment of power residues from the Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (published in Commentationes arithmeticae 1849 and Opera Posthuma 1862). It is well discussed by historians (e.g. Weil) as a precursor of Lagrange's theorem and group cosets. It is a nice but known treatment, not new.

checkable.asserts: Number of distinct biquadratic residues mod prime p=4q+1 is q (n = q).

checkable.asserts: For p=29, x=2 (x^2=4 not a quartic residue), classes R, xR, x^2R, x^3R partition 1..28 and are disjoint.

checkable.asserts: Coset multiplication table of §430 for p=37: I·III ⊂ R, I·I ⊂ II, II·III ⊂ I.

checkable.asserts: §431–432: the quadratic residues mod 17 are exactly R ∪ x^2R (x=3, x^2=9 not a quartic residue).

transcription_corrections: No substantive transcription errors found. The printed §428 itself reads 'foret βx² — αx, ideoque βx — α per 4q+1 divisibile' (the word 'divisibile' is shared, an ellipsis of the original, not a transcription error). §430 'in tertia classi' matches the print.
